title: Bonfire Night
strapline: Fireworks bursting across the dark like flowers — and a safe, sparkly way to make our own, well away from any flame.
intent: Bonfire Night is a burst of light, colour and sound in the November dark that many children witness from a distance, and provision that recreates it safely lets them explore the wonder while learning that fire and fireworks are for grown-ups to handle.
Making firework art with colour and movement is expressive, creative and fine-motor work — splattering, swirling, scratching, sprinkling.
Firework patterns are full of mathematics — starbursts and spirals, counting explosions, high and low, big and small, sequences of bangs.
Firework safety is real, important knowledge for young children — stay back, watch from a distance, sparklers only with a grown-up holding on — woven in gently, not fearfully.
The night pours in language for light and sound — sparkle, burst, whizz, bang, glitter, swirl, colour, dark.
Sharing the excitement, and caring for those who find the noise frightening — including pets — grows empathy and community.
implementation: Recreate the sparkle safely indoors — firework paintings with splatter, glitter, chalk on black paper, torches in the dark, ribbon 'sparklers' to wave.
Talk about staying safe warmly and clearly: 'Fireworks are beautiful, but they're very hot — we always watch from far away, and only grown-ups touch them.'
Model the colour and pattern talk: 'Your firework's bursting out in every direction — how many colours can you see in it?'
Bring in maths through the play — count the bursts, make big and small explosions, repeat a spiral pattern, sequence the whizz-then-bang.
Explore the sound safely — soft and loud, a slow whizz building to a bang on instruments — and talk about how the noise can be scary, and how we help pets and friends who find it too much.
Keep everything flame-free and calm — no real sparklers or fires with the children — and let those who prefer quiet watching do so.
key_questions: Your firework is bursting out in every direction — how many colours can you see?
Why do you think we always watch fireworks from far away?
Can you make a big burst and then a tiny one?
How does the noise make you feel — and how could we help someone who finds it scary?
What sound does your firework make — a whizz, or a bang?

impact.text: Children create firework art with colour and movement — splattering, swirling, scratching, sprinkling.
Children explore starbursts and spirals, counting explosions and making them big and small.
Children take on real, gently-taught safety knowledge — stay back, watch from a distance, grown-ups only.
Children gain words for light and sound — sparkle, burst, whizz, bang, glitter, swirl.
Children share the excitement and care for those — including pets — who find the noise frightening.

enhancements: Firework paintings with splatter, glitter and chalk on black paper.
Torches in the dark and ribbon 'sparklers' to wave — everything flame-free.
Instruments for a slow whizz building to a bang, exploring soft and loud safely.
A quiet watching corner for children who prefer calm.
A talk about how we help pets and friends who find the noise too much.

playing_exploring: Children recreate the colour, light and sound of fireworks safely, exploring a spectacle they know from a distance.
They splatter, swirl and wave their way into making their own bursts of light.
active_learning: Children stay absorbed in perfecting their firework art and sounds, working at getting the burst just right.
creating_thinking: Children invent firework patterns and sounds, and take on real knowledge about staying safe near fire and fireworks.
